records.text: A 2018 book asked prominent AI researchers when human-level AI might arrive; the closest predicted date was 2029, and most placed it fifty years away.
AI progress has accelerated since late 2022.
Frontier AI labs now use their own AI models to create better AI models.
In Greek mythology, Hephaestus built a bronze giant named Talos who guarded Crete by throwing rocks at enemy ships.
The ancient Greeks already had accurate long-range projectile weapons.
Automatically recognising an enemy ship is a classic computer vision problem that proved far harder for humanity than the rock-throwing part.
In the Judean legend, wise rabbis created golems who could understand and obey but could not speak, because speech was thought to require a soul.
Today, speech synthesis is far easier than speech recognition, which is the opposite of the myth.
Al-Jazari (12th century), the automata at Hesdin Castle, and Leonardo da Vinci's mechanical knight were early automata.
Pierre Jaquet-Droz's 18th-century calligrapher was a programmable doll that wrote different letters via a system of levers on its back.
The 18th-century calligrapher automaton was the first programmable device, predating Jacquard looms and punched cards.
The calligrapher automaton was purely mechanical; mathematical or logical intelligence remained rudimentary for centuries.
Ramon Llull's logical machine was a notable early effort in logical intelligence, though its significance is stretched.
AI as a science began with Alan Turing's 1950 paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence".
The original Turing test involves a judge chatting in writing with two hidden entities—a human and a computer—and having to distinguish them.
A single run of the Turing test is meaningless; the computer program passes only when, over many trials, the judge cannot distinguish it from a human with probability different from ½.
The Turing test is placed in the realm of probability theory and randomized algorithms.
The Turing test survived longer than almost any other AI benchmark.
The Turing test was formally passed only in 2025, after models like GPT-4 could be made to stay in character and fool judges in extended conversations.
AI has a long history of moving goalposts: when Deep Blue beat Kasparov, chess was dismissed as "just tree search"; when AlphaGo mastered Go, the bar shifted again.
The Turing test resisted because it hinges on free-form natural language.
A judge in the Turing test can ask anything—demand a drawing, describe a 3D scene, request a joke about a specific topic.
To maintain consistency in the Turing test, the computer must understand the physical world and a vast range of human knowledge.
Natural language is complete in the sense that it can express any query about the world.
Large language models are powerful because to predict the next token well they must internalise an enormous amount of world structure.
Robotics is a notable exception to large language models' world understanding, because we lack large text corpora describing low-level motor actions.
The Turing test is fundamentally unfair to computers: in a reverse Turing test, a human would fail immediately because a 1950s computer could instantly compute $37^{23}$.
Turing's original essay included a detail about gender impersonation that has often been forgotten.
The Turing test got people thinking about what intelligence requires.
AI as an academic field was born in 1956 at the Dartmouth workshop.
The Dartmouth workshop was organized by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon, and Nathaniel Rochester.
The grant proposal for the Dartmouth workshop is probably the most ambitious in computing history.
The Dartmouth workshop proposal conjectured that every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can be precisely described so that a machine can simulate it.
The Dartmouth workshop proposal aimed to make machines use natural language, form abstractions and concepts, solve problems reserved for humans, and improve themselves.
The Dartmouth workshop took place, but the participants mainly began to grasp how difficult the problems were.
The Logic Theorist successfully re-proved most of Principia Mathematica, sometimes more elegantly than Russell and Whitehead.
The General Problem Solver was an early AI program that tried to think like a human.
Specialised early AI programs operated in microworlds: Analogy solved IQ tests, Student handled algebraic word problems, and Blocks World simulated 3D block manipulation.
The 1960s ended with disappointment in AI, especially after the failure of machine-translation projects, leading to the first "AI winter".
During the AI winter, the only active AI branch was expert systems.
MYCIN was a medical diagnosis expert system for blood infections.
A blood test yields about 50 numerical indicators.
A physician uses local heuristics such as "if red blood cell count is high and iron is low, then disease X" to diagnose.
The challenge in expert systems is that terms like "high" are fuzzy and many rules partially apply.
MYCIN had about 450 rules.
MYCIN performed as well as experienced physicians and significantly better than novices.
The first AI department at DEC reportedly saved the company around $10 million annually by 1986.
The AI boom of the 1980s ended in the late 80s when many companies failed to meet inflated expectations.
In the 1990s, the focus of AI shifted to learning from data, accelerated by the growth of the Internet.
Early neural networks (convolutional, recurrent, deep) existed conceptually but lacked data and compute.

The deep-learning revolution took off in the mid-2000s when labs, notably Geoffrey Hinton's and Yoshua Bengio's, gained access to internet-scale data and computational power, especially GPUs with thousands of cores.
GPUs have thousands of cores that make the parallelisable operations of neural networks feasible.
Deep learning has set the state of the art in many fields since the late 2000s, culminating in the LLM revolution.
A computer program learns from experience $E$ with respect to a class of tasks $T$ and a performance measure $P$, if its performance on tasks in $T$ (measured by $P$) improves with experience $E$.
The key to the definition of learning is having a number that goes up or down to measure performance.
Half of deep learning consists of inventing loss functions—deciding what number to minimise so that minimising it yields the desired behaviour.
Supervised learning learns from a set of labelled examples, each consisting of features $X$ and a correct answer $Y$, the response variable to predict.
The response variable $Y$ can be categorical, continuous, or ordinal.
The model learns a function $f(X)$ meant to match $Y$.
Mathematically, supervised learning aims to learn the conditional distribution $p(y \mid x)$.
In supervised learning, the input vector $X$ is often high-dimensional, while the output $Y$ is relatively simple.
The main goal of supervised learning is generalisation to new examples; failure to generalise leads to overfitting.
Generalisation is checked via cross-validation, which splits data into training and validation sets.
Preprocessing and feature extraction often precede modelling in supervised learning.
Classification is a supervised learning task that assigns a discrete class, e.g., spam filtering or face recognition.
Regression is a supervised learning task that predicts the value of an unknown function, e.g., stock prices or speech recognition.
Collecting labels, especially for tasks like image segmentation, is often extremely expensive, so supervised learning often works with relatively small labelled datasets.
Unsupervised learning learns from data without labels, using only raw data.
Clustering is an unsupervised task that partitions data into groups based on similarity, with applications like gene families or user personalisation.
Dimensionality reduction is an unsupervised task that selects or extracts the most informative features from high-dimensional data.
An image of 1 megapixel with 3 colour channels is a point in a space of approximately 3 million dimensions.
The set of real images forms a very complicated manifold in high-dimensional space.
Unsupervised learning tries to compress the image manifold to a manageable size (e.g., 500 dimensions) while preserving the ability to answer interesting questions.
In the compressed space, classes like cats and dogs might become linearly separable.
Matrix completion is an unsupervised task that predicts missing entries in a sparse matrix.
A natural framework for unsupervised learning is the autoencoder: an encoder network compresses input $x$ to a low-dimensional code $z$, and a decoder network tries to reconstruct $\hat{x}$ from $z$.
The loss function in an autoencoder is simply the reconstruction error, e.g., $(\hat{x} - x)^2$.
The autoencoder learns to encode information that matters for reconstruction.
Clustering can be viewed as an extreme case of autoencoding: compressing each point to a discrete label (zero-dimensional code) and reconstructing using the cluster centre.
Supervised learning models $p(y \mid x)$; unsupervised learning models $p(x)$ itself, often yielding generative models that can produce new samples from the data distribution.
Reinforcement learning involves an agent learning from its own trial-and-error interactions with an environment.
Multi-armed bandits is a fundamental challenge in reinforcement learning: choosing actions that lead to random rewards to maximise cumulative reward.
Exploration vs. exploitation is a fundamental challenge in reinforcement learning: deciding when to try new actions versus stick with known good ones.
Credit assignment is a fundamental challenge in reinforcement learning: assigning credit to individual actions when the reward is delayed.
This lecture course does not cover reinforcement learning.
Active learning involves choosing the next data point to label, often because labelling is expensive.
Learning to rank produces ordered lists, e.g., for internet search results.
Bootstrapping uses a model's own outputs to improve itself.
Model selection involves balancing models with few versus many parameters.
Methods that not only give an answer but also estimate confidence, describe data quality, and anticipate changes with further experiments rely on probability theory.
In machine learning, the probability spaces are Euclidean spaces $\mathbb{R}^d$ with a density; no measure theory or exotic spaces are needed.
Joint probability $p(x, y)$ is the probability of two events occurring simultaneously.
Marginalisation computes $p(x) = \sum_y p(x, y)$ (or an integral for continuous variables).
Conditional probability is defined as $p(x \mid y) = \frac{p(x, y)}{p(y)}$, provided $p(y) > 0$.
Bayes' theorem states $p(y \mid x) = \frac{p(x \mid y)\, p(y)}{p(x)} = \frac{p(x \mid y)\, p(y)}{\sum_{y'} p(x \mid y')\, p(y')}$.
Random variables $x$ and $y$ are independent if $p(x, y) = p(x)\, p(y)$, which implies $p(x \mid y) = p(x)$.
For parameter estimation, Bayes' theorem reads $p(\theta \mid D) = \frac{p(\theta)\, p(D \mid \theta)}{p(D)}$.
$p(\theta)$ is the prior distribution, representing beliefs about $\theta$ before seeing data.
$p(D \mid \theta)$ is the likelihood, the probability/density of the observed dataset given the parameters.
$p(\theta \mid D)$ is the posterior distribution, the updated belief after seeing data.
$p(D) = \int p(D \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)\, \mathrm{d}\theta$ is the evidence, a normalising constant usually inaccessible.
Because $p(D)$ does not involve $\theta$, the posterior is proportional to the product of likelihood and prior: $p(\theta \mid D) \propto p(D \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)$.
Maximum likelihood (ML) estimation selects $\theta_{\text{ML}} = \arg\max_\theta p(D \mid \theta)$.
Maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation selects $\theta_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\max_\theta p(\theta \mid D) = \arg\max_\theta p(D \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)$.
The logarithm of the posterior is $\log p(D \mid \theta) + \log p(\theta) + \text{constant}$.
In optimisation, $\log p(\theta)$ acts as a regulariser, penalising parameter values that are unlikely a priori.
This provides a direct bridge from Bayesian inference to deep learning regularisation.
A direct problem: given a probabilistic model, predict behaviour; e.g., an urn with 10 balls, 3 black, what is the probability of drawing a black ball?
An inverse problem: observe behaviour and infer hidden parameters; e.g., an urn is known to have either 3 or 6 black balls, you draw a black ball, what is the probability it was the first urn?
Machine learning problems are almost always inverse: we observe data and must build a probabilistic model of the hidden variables that generated it.
Classical probability interprets probability as the limit of relative frequencies over repeated experiments, such as coin tosses.
We often want to reason about unique events, such as 'Spain wins the 2026 World Cup' or 'the Odyssey was written by a woman', where infinite repetitions are meaningless.
In such cases, probability becomes a degree of belief.
The Bayesian interpretation of probability follows the same mathematical laws as frequency-based probability.
In the two children problem, a person has two kids, each equally likely a boy or a girl.
One question in the two children problem: if the person answers 'yes' to 'Do you have any boys?', what is the probability of also having a girl?
Another question in the two children problem: if you meet one of the kids and it's a boy, what is the probability the other is a girl?
In the prosecutor's fallacy example, a rare blood type with 1% prevalence is found at a crime scene and matches the defendant.
The prosecutor might argue that there is only a 1% chance of a match if the defendant is innocent, so with 99% probability he is guilty.

The prosecutor's argument is mistaken because the probability of guilt is not 1 minus the probability of a match given innocence; it requires the prior probability of guilt and consideration of all alternative suspects.
The defense might counter that a million people live in the city, so 10,000 have this blood type, and thus the blood only gives a 0.01% probability of guilt.
The defense's argument is mistaken because all those 10,000 people together still account for only a small fraction of the city; the evidence is not worthless.

The O.J. Simpson trial and the Sally Clark case (involving two sudden infant death syndrome deaths) both involved misapplied probability where the court sometimes confused conditional probabilities and ignored base rates.
In the Bayesian inference for a coin, we have an unfair coin with unknown probability $p_h = \theta$ of heads.
Flipping the coin $N$ times yields a sequence $s$ with $n$ heads and $m$ tails.
Assuming flips are independent given $\theta$, the likelihood is $p(s \mid \theta) = \theta^n (1 - \theta)^m$.
In machine learning, defining the model means writing down the likelihood, specifying the assumptions (mutually exclusive outcomes, conditional independence) that produce the formula.
Defining the likelihood is the easy part of machine learning modeling.
Maximising the likelihood directly gives $\theta_{\text{ML}} = \frac{n}{n+m}$.
For a coin with many tosses, the maximum likelihood estimate matches the frequency limit and is correct.
If we toss the coin once and get tails, the maximum likelihood estimate is $\theta = 0$, implying the coin always lands tails.
After a single toss, the conclusion that the coin always lands tails is absurd; the estimate is unreliable because we have almost no data.
In real machine learning, data is almost always insufficient.
When you have enough data for your current model, it is often better to move to a larger model (e.g., from GPT-1 to GPT-2) for which you are again data-limited.
We constantly operate at the frontier where data is scarce.
A point estimate based on the likelihood alone is rarely enough in machine learning.
We need to bring in prior beliefs.
Bayes’ rule gives the posterior $p(\theta \mid s) = \frac{p(s \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)}{p(s)}$.
The prior $p(\theta)$ represents what was believed about $\theta$ before seeing the data.
For a coin, the most basic reasonable belief is that $\theta$ must lie in $[0,1]$, so $p(\theta) = 0$ outside that interval.
A common uninformative choice is a uniform prior $p(\theta) = 1$ for $\theta \in [0,1]$, expressing complete ignorance.
With $n$ heads and $m$ tails, the posterior with a uniform prior is $p(\theta \mid s) = \frac{\theta^n (1 - \theta)^m}{\int_0^1 \theta^n (1 - \theta)^m \, \mathrm{d}\theta}$.
The denominator in the posterior is a Beta integral, $B(n+1, m+1) = \frac{n!\, m!}{(n+m+1)!}$, but for point estimation only the proportionality is needed.
Maximising the posterior with a uniform prior yields the same estimate as maximum likelihood: $\theta_{\text{MAP}} = \frac{n}{n+m}$.
The uniform prior rules out degenerate solutions, e.g., $\theta=0$ or $\theta=1$ with a single observation would give a posterior of 0, but does not change the location of the maximum.
MAP with a uniform prior does not fix the overconfidence of the point estimate when data is scarce.
The ultimate goal in Bayesian inference is not the parameter $\theta$ but prediction.
Given past data, we want the probability of the next outcome, $p(\text{heads} \mid s)$.

The probability of the next outcome does not depend on $\theta$; it is obtained by averaging the likelihood over the posterior: $p(\text{heads} \mid s) = \int_0^1 p(\text{heads} \mid \theta)\, p(\theta \mid s)\, \mathrm{d}\theta$.
Evaluating the integral gives Laplace’s rule of succession: $p(\text{heads} \mid s) = \frac{n+1}{n+m+2}$.
Even with a uniform prior, the predictive distribution is different from the point estimate $\frac{n}{n+m}$.
For example, after one tail ($n=0, m=1$) the point estimate is $0$, but Laplace’s rule gives $\frac{1}{3}$, a more reasonable belief.
As data accumulates, the predictive distribution and the point estimate converge, but with little data the advantage of averaging over the whole posterior is decisive.
The predictive distribution is the expectation over the posterior of the likelihood.
The predictive distribution is almost always what we want from a machine learning system.
In neural networks, the parameters $\theta$ are the weights, and we care about predictions on new images, not the weights themselves.
The Bayesian framework makes focusing on predictive distributions natural.
When data is limited, the prior heavily influences the conclusion.
A more realistic prior for a physical coin might be a bell-shaped curve centred near $\frac{1}{2}$, such as a truncated normal.
Multiplying a bell-shaped prior by the polynomial likelihood $\theta^n (1-\theta)^m$ yields an expression that is not a standard distribution and is tractable only numerically.
We can choose a prior that is mathematically convenient, provided it captures rough features like being bounded between 0 and 1 and peaked near $\frac{1}{2}$.
This leads directly to the idea of conjugate priors.
In Bayesian inference, after choosing the likelihood, a prior $p(\theta)$ must also be chosen.
The prior is a distribution over all possible parameter values, and its shape strongly affects the results, especially with small datasets.
To simplify computation, we want the posterior $p(\theta \mid x)$ to belong to the same parametric family as the prior $p(\theta)$.
If the posterior belongs to the same family, we can update hyperparameters directly without new integrals.

A family of distributions $p(\theta \mid \alpha)$ is a conjugate prior for a family of likelihoods $p(x \mid \theta)$ if, after multiplying by the likelihood, the posterior stays in the same family: $p(\theta \mid x, \alpha) = p(\theta \mid \alpha')$.
The $\alpha$ are called hyperparameters — the parameters of the distribution of the parameters.
The trivial family of all distributions is conjugate, but it is not useful.
The form of a useful conjugate prior depends on the form of the data likelihood.
For Bernoulli (coin-toss) trials, the likelihood is proportional to $\theta^s (1-\theta)^f$ with $s$ successes and $f$ failures.

The conjugate prior for Bernoulli trials is the Beta distribution: $p(\theta \mid \alpha, \beta) = \frac{\theta^{\alpha-1} (1-\theta)^{\beta-1}}{B(\alpha, \beta)}$, with $B(\alpha, \beta) = \frac{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}$, for $\theta \in [0,1]$.

After observing $s$ heads and $f$ tails, the posterior is proportional to $\theta^{s + \alpha - 1} (1-\theta)^{f + \beta - 1}$, which is again a Beta distribution, $\text{Beta}(s+\alpha, \, f+\beta)$.
The learning rule is: add the counts to the hyperparameters: $\alpha' = \alpha + s$, $\beta' = \beta + f$.
The hyperparameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ can be interpreted as pseudo-counts—fictitious prior observations.
The uniform prior corresponds to $\alpha = \beta = 1$ ($\text{Beta}(1,1)$).
A prior peaked around $\frac{1}{2}$ is obtained by setting, for example, $\alpha = \beta = 10$, encoding the belief that we have already seen virtually 10 heads and 10 tails.
It takes a substantial amount of real data to shift the posterior away from $\frac{1}{2}$ when the prior is peaked.

Because the posterior has the same form as the prior, Bayesian updating can be done sequentially: start with a prior, incorporate a data batch, obtain a posterior, then treat that posterior as the new prior for the next batch, avoiding reprocessing all data from scratch.
The predictive distribution for a new trial, using a Beta$(\alpha, \beta)$ prior, generalises Laplace’s rule: $p(\text{heads} \mid s, f) = \frac{s + \alpha}{s + f + \alpha + \beta}$.
A natural extension of coin tossing is rolling a die with $k$ faces, modelled by a multinomial distribution.

For a multinomial distribution, if $x_i$ observations fall into category $i$, the likelihood is $p(x \mid \theta) \propto \theta_1^{x_1} \theta_2^{x_2} \dots \theta_k^{x_k}$, with $\sum_i \theta_i = 1$.
The conjugate prior for the multinomial distribution is the Dirichlet distribution: $p(\theta \mid \alpha) \propto \theta_1^{\alpha_1-1} \theta_2^{\alpha_2-1} \dots \theta_k^{\alpha_k-1}$.

After observing counts $x_1, \dots, x_k$, the hyperparameters update analogously: $p(\theta \mid x, \alpha) = p(\theta \mid x + \alpha) \propto \theta_1^{x_1+\alpha_1-1} \theta_2^{x_2+\alpha_2-1} \dots \theta_k^{x_k+\alpha_k-1}$.
The simplicity of updating makes conjugate priors a cornerstone of tractable Bayesian inference.
